name: Adam Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, I'm 27, and I manage seven transport planners at a big logistics company's distribution hub outside town. We plan the routes and loading slots for about sixty trucks a day going out to supermarkets. I live with my partner Sofia, who's doing a master's in public health and works weekends in a coffee shop, so money's tight until she finishes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven with the overnight problems: a driver off sick, a truck stuck at the port, a store that's changed its delivery window. My team rebuilds the plan, and I sit between them and the warehouse floor managers, who all think planners live in a fantasy world. I use AI every day, for drafting emails, checking the route plans and summing up the weekly numbers for my boss. I love solving the puzzle; I hate the 6 a.m. phone calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it out loud that it was oversold, but the tools are still useful. I use them every day and they save me maybe an hour. I'd post something like, nice tool, not a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I've bet a lot of my energy on it. But the real issue for me wouldn't change: my pay is low for this role, and Sofia's tuition takes most of what's left. We've got about two weeks of money in the bank after her last fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I use and push the company to let my team use them too. I'd ask for the pay rise I was promised when I took on the extra planners last year. And I'd keep an eye out for planning jobs in the city, though that's an hour's drive each way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about work, tight about money. AI isn't what keeps me up at night. The car insurance renewal next month is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you push the company to let your team use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now only managers get the AI licences, because of the cost. My planners copy things into their phones on the sly, which is a data risk. I'd ask IT to give the whole team proper licences, it would pay for itself in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money is tight until Sofia finishes. When does that ease?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next summer, if she gets a job in public health straight away, which isn't a sure thing. Until then, one big repair bill sinks us. Last winter the boiler went and we put it on a credit card we're still paying off.

say: I'd say they save me **an hour** a day, which is nice but not a revolution.
think: I'd be a bit **disappointed** after betting energy on AI.
The real pressure is **low pay** and Sofia's tuition, not technology.
do: Push IT for **AI licences** for the whole planning team.
Ask for the **pay rise** promised when the team grew.
Watch for **planning jobs** in the city, an hour away.
feel: **Fine about work** but tight and watchful about money.
S0.quote: AI isn't what keeps me up at night. The car insurance renewal next month is.
fieldNote: He is the **keenest AI user** among the people he describes at work.
His stress is a **credit card** debt and partner's tuition, not his job.
He'd push for **team licences**, thinking about data risk and fairness.

steps.text: Ask IT for AI licences for all seven planners
Ask his boss for the pay rise promised last year
Pay down the boiler credit card before anything else

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it publicly: this is coming, so let's do it fairly. At work I'd volunteer to lead the AI planning pilot, but I'd also say staff should share in the savings. Online I'd argue for things like a shorter week rather than layoffs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine, maybe even better off, because I'm the one who already knows the tools. But planning is on the card, and my seven planners would probably become three or four. I'd be keeping my job by shrinking my own team, and I don't feel great about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my boss with a plan to run route planning with AI and fewer people, but with the spare people moved into the warehouse or customer roles instead of let go. I'd take any course they offered on the new planning system. And I'd start doing a bit of freelance setup work on weekends for small hauliers who can't afford a consultant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty at the same time. I like the work, but these are people I eat lunch with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd freelance for small hauliers. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are loads of firms with five or ten trucks still planning routes on a whiteboard. I could set up a cheap AI planning tool for them for a few hundred each. Even two jobs a month would cover our car and insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine, but your team shrinks. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I'd be fine on paper, but the people who go would be my friends. Priya, my most experienced planner, has a mortgage and two kids, and I'd be the one whose plan cut her job.

say: The change is **coming**, so let's do it **fairly**.
Staff should **share the savings**, through things like a shorter working week.
think: Knowing the tools probably keeps **my job safe**, maybe better paid.
My team of seven likely shrinks to **three or four**.
do: Pitch a plan to **redeploy planners** to the warehouse rather than lay them off.
Take any course on the **new planning system**.
Set up AI planning for **small hauliers** on weekends.
feel: **Excited and guilty**, because the people affected are lunch friends.
S1.quote: I'd be keeping my job by shrinking my own team, and I don't feel great about that.
fieldNote: He sees himself as a **winner** of this picture and doesn't hide it.
He pairs automation with a **redeployment** idea to ease his conscience.
A **side business** for small hauliers fits his money gap and skills.

steps.text: Lead the hub's AI route planning pilot
Propose moving spare planners into warehouse roles instead of layoffs
Set up AI planning tools for small hauliers on weekends
Take the course on the new planning system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and governments need to act this year, not in five. I'd be pushing for a tax on companies replacing staff to fund basic income. I'd be loud about it, because I know how quickly a hub like ours could run itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, knowing the tools doesn't save me if the tools can do my job too. AGI means the planning, the reporting, even managing the exceptions goes to software. The warehouse floor lasts until the robots around 2031, so the people I used to think were less safe would actually outlast me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd save hard, maybe two hundred a month, and pay off the boiler card. I'd ask to move onto the warehouse side, managing the floor team, because hands-on work gives me those three extra years. And I'd learn whatever comes next, maybe robot fleet management, since someone has to run the robots in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. I'm the guy who loves this stuff, and even I can see I'd be out of a job with two weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move to the warehouse floor rather than stay with planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning is pure thinking work and goes on day one. The floor still needs someone to run the shifts, sort out the forklifts and deal with people for a few years. The warehouse floor is a step sideways in pay but a step forward in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if Sofia hasn't found work by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're in real trouble, because her coffee shop money only covers food. Public health jobs might be safer than mine, there'll be a lot of public health problems. But if neither of us has a proper job in 2028, we'd probably have to move back in with my parents.

say: Governments must act **this year**, not in five.
A **tax on replacing staff** should fund a basic income.
think: AGI takes **planning and reporting**, so knowing the tools won't save me.
Warehouse staff would **outlast me** until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Save **two hundred a month** and clear the boiler credit card.
Move to managing the **warehouse floor** to gain three years.
Learn **robot fleet management** before robots arrive.
feel: **Alarmed**, because even an AI fan sees his job vanishing.
S2.quote: The warehouse floor is a step sideways in pay but a step forward in time.
fieldNote: He clearly grasps the **three-year gap** and moves toward hands-on work.
He notices the **irony** that floor staff outlast the planners.
Moving back to **his parents** is his fallback if Sofia has no job.

steps.text: Save two hundred a month and clear the boiler card
Apply to manage the hub's warehouse floor team
Take a course in robot fleet management
Campaign for a tax on firms that replace staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if companies are honest about plans. I'd ask the union at our hub to get a deal on retraining before the first job cuts. I'd keep posting about basic income because I think it's the only thing that scales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use the next five years to get as far ahead as I can. I'd be the one who builds the AI planning system, and then I'd move on before it replaces me. By 2031 I'd want to be in a robotics or automation role, which gives me until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take an evening course in industrial automation, about two years part-time. I'd grow the freelance work with small hauliers so it's a real second income by 2029. And I'd start a small savings pot with Sofia once she has a job, aiming for three months by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty driven, honestly, with a bit of fear underneath. Five years is enough to get moving but not enough to coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd build the system that replaces you. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortably. But if I don't build the system, the company hires a consultant who doesn't care about my best planner Priya or anyone. At least I'd fight for the redeployment bit while I'm in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the freelance work grow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Word of mouth among small hauliers, mostly, they all know each other. If one firm saves money on fuel because of my setup, they tell the next. I'd need a cheap laptop and a weekend a month.

say: Five years is **short but workable** with honest companies.
The hub union should secure **retraining deals** before any cuts.
think: I'd **build the AI system**, then move on before it replaces me.
By 2031 I want an **automation role**, safe until about 2034.
do: Take a **two-year evening course** in industrial automation.
Grow the **freelance hauliers** work into a real second income by 2029.
Build **three months of savings** with Sofia by 2030.
feel: **Driven**, with a bit of fear underneath.
S3.quote: If I don't build the system, the company hires a consultant who doesn't care about my best planner Priya or anyone.
fieldNote: He plans to **stay one step ahead** of the machine he builds.
He still argues for **redeployment** of colleagues from inside the room.
His freelance plan is **concrete**: word of mouth among small hauliers.

steps.text: Take a two-year evening course in industrial automation
Grow freelance AI setups for small hauliers by 2029
Build three months of savings with Sofia by 2030
Build the hub's AI planning system himself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and wasting it would be a scandal. I'd push for a national retraining scheme, paid properly, so warehouse and office workers can switch. I'd be the guy at parties going on about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough for me to change careers fully. I'd be 37, with Sofia working, maybe savings, maybe a kid. The end point is still scary, but there's time to get to the robotics side or into public service work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the hub for three or four years, run the automation, and save. Then I'd move into a robotics or automation engineering job, maybe in the city. I'd invest a little in an index fund each month once we've got three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little uneasy. I'd be thinking about it, but not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have kids in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, around 31 or 32. I'd want us both in jobs that last until at least the robots. A decade's warning makes having kids feel possible, once my partner Sofia's career is settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning moving to the city. Would you actually go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, eventually, there are only so many logistics jobs around here. Sofia would have more public health jobs there too. We'd just need enough savings to cover the deposit and the first month's rent.

We need a **national retraining scheme**, paid properly.
think: Ten years is enough to **change careers** fully.
Robotics or **public service** work could carry me past AGI.

fieldNote: The decade turns AGI into a **career plan** for him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because even I couldn't stay ahead of it with two weeks of savings. What would help is a basic income, or at least a proper wage while you retrain, plus companies paying a share of the savings back to the people they replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people in my spot. Middle managers like me are both the ones bringing the AI in and the ones it's coming for. That's a weird place to be at 27.

headlineQuote: Middle managers like me are both the ones bringing the AI in and the ones it's coming for.
portrait: Adam is 27 and manages **seven transport planners** at a big logistics hub.
He uses AI daily and would **lead the automation** at work, with some guilt.
His partner Sofia is a **student**, and they have two weeks of savings and a credit card debt.
He stays uneasy until **fast AGI** turns his own planning job into a target.
His plans move toward **hands-on automation** work, side income and the city.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even his tool skills can't outrun it with tiny savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or paid retraining wage.
Companies sharing **automation savings** with the workers they replace.
